summary: This document defines five parameters for the tel URI that carry number portability information. They can be passed to the next-hop network node after a number portability database lookup has been performed.

plainLanguage.summary: When a person keeps their phone number but changes phone company, calls must be routed correctly. This adds notes to the phone-number link recording where the number now lives.

subtitle: Five extra parameters that let a phone-number link carry number portability routing hints between trusted call-handling nodes.

tldr.problem: When a phone number has been ported to another carrier, a node that looks up the new routing information has no standard way to pass the result to the next node, which would then repeat the lookup.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4694 adds five parameters to the tel URI (rn, rn-context, npdi, cic and cic-context) that carry the routing number, a flag saying the database lookup was already done, and the freephone carrier code.
tldr.outcome: Trusted nodes can route calls from the parameters instead of repeating lookups, but the parameters only make sense inside a circle of trust and should not appear in static content.

facts.label: Repeats allowed
facts.value: rn, npdi and cic at most once each

facts.label: Processing order
facts.value: cic, then rn, then the number

today: RFC 4694 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says further information on a registry for the parameters is covered in a separate Work in Progress document.

sections.title: Why Portability Needs URI Parameters
sections.content:
Number portability (NP) lets telephone subscribers keep their numbers when they change service provider, move to a new location or change the services they subscribe to. It applies to geographical numbers, mobile numbers, freephone (toll-free) numbers and other non-geographical numbers.

Portability affects call signaling and routing. After a node has done an NP database lookup (a "dip"), the result has to travel in the tel URI used by protocols such as SIP and H.323. A Voice over IP server can then use the information in a received tel URI to decide where to route the call.

RFC 4694 defines five parameters for that job, extending the tel URI of RFC 3966. Number portability itself is described in RFC 3482.
sections.plainLanguage: If you move house but keep your phone number, the post office needs a note saying where you really live now. These parameters are that note, stuck onto the phone number so the next person does not have to look it up again.

sections.title: The Five Parameters and Their Syntax
sections.content:
The parameters extend the parameter rule of the tel URI using ABNF. Each of rn, npdi and cic can appear at most once in a URI.

  • rn carries a routing number. A routing number is associated with a geographical or mobile number that has been ported out from a donor carrier to another carrier. It can also identify the switch or network node that originates a call.
  • rn-context says how to interpret a local rn value.
  • npdi is a flag with no value. It is the NP database dip indicator: it tells downstream nodes that the lookup has already been done.
  • cic carries a Carrier Identification Code, which identifies the current freephone service provider for a freephone number.
  • cic-context says how to interpret a local cic value.

Both rn and cic come in a global form and a local form. A global value starts with + and MUST begin with a valid E.164 country code. A local value must be interpreted using its context parameter, which holds either a domain name or a global number. Visual separators (hyphens, dots and parentheses) are optional.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five labels you can stick on a phone number: where to send the call, how to read that address, a tick saying "already checked", the name of the toll-free company, and how to read that name.

sections.title: Handling a Received URI
sections.content:
These parameters are for call signaling between nodes that trust each other. When a tel URI appears in static content such as an HTML page or a presence document, the parameters SHOULD NOT be present, and an entity that receives them SHOULD remove them. A node that receives a message from an element it does not trust SHOULD ignore the parameters, and MAY redo the database query.

The processing order is: look at cic first, then rn, and finally the number itself.

  • If the URI has npdi, the node MUST NOT look up NP information for a geographical number, even if it is set up to do so.
  • If cic names a carrier associated with this node, the node MUST ignore it and look at rn. It MUST remove cic when routing to a next hop that belongs to another carrier. Otherwise it MUST route on the CIC.
  • If rn points to this node, the node routes on the telephone number and MUST remove rn when setting up the next hop. If rn points to a network this node is in, it routes on the number, MAY query the NP database, and MUST remove rn if the next hop belongs to another carrier. Otherwise it MUST route on rn.

If a node does not know how to route on cic or rn, local policy MUST decide whether to stop or to continue while ignoring the unknown information.
sections.plainLanguage: When a call arrives with these notes, the node reads the toll-free company note first, then the new-address note, and only then the plain phone number. It peels off a note once the call has reached the place the note pointed to.

sections.title: Adding Parameters After a Lookup
sections.content:
For a geographical number, a node that queries an NP database MUST add rn when it gets a routing number back, and MUST also add npdi. If there is no routing number, for example for a non-ported number, it MUST add just npdi.

For a freephone number, two database accesses normally happen. The first, by the originating network, finds the CIC of the serving freephone provider. The second, at that provider, maps the freephone number to a geographical number.

  • If the CIC belongs to the node's own provider, or says a geographic number is supplied, the node MUST NOT add cic and MUST replace the freephone number with the geographical number.
  • If the CIC belongs to another freephone provider, the node MUST add cic.
  • If a geographical number is returned together with NP information, the node MUST add npdi, and rn only when a routing number is available.

A node that is first to handle a call request MAY also put an rn in the URI associated with the caller, for example from the Jurisdiction Information Parameter of an SS7 ISUP message. That value may not be authenticated, so using it for charging is done at the recipient's own risk.
sections.plainLanguage: After looking up where a number really lives, the node writes the answer on the number and ticks the "already checked" box so nobody else has to look again. For toll-free numbers it first writes the company name, and later swaps in a normal number.

sections.title: Gateways Between ISUP and VoIP
sections.content:
A gateway between SS7 ISUP and a VoIP protocol such as SIP or H.323 MUST map between ISUP parameters and these URI parameters for routing, and MAY do so for the URI associated with the caller. The RFC covers only the American National Standards Institute (ANSI) ISUP case, since ISUP support for NP depends on the country.

  • For a ported number, the routing number in the ISUP Called Party Number becomes rn, and the number marked as the ported number in the Generic Address Parameter goes into the URI's number part.
  • For a non-ported number, the Called Party Number goes into the number part, and rn MUST NOT appear unless local policy requires it.
  • The gateway MUST include npdi when the Ported Number Translation Indicator bit in the Forward Call Indicator is set to 1.
  • It MUST include cic when the ISUP Carrier Identification Parameter is present.

Mapping in the other direction, from URI parameters back into ISUP, depends on national ISUP implementations and is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Old phone switches and internet phone systems speak different languages. A gateway translates the sticky notes between the two so neither side loses the information.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives seven examples. In the first, a freephone number tel:+1-800-123-4567 served by a provider with CIC +1-6789 becomes tel:+1-800-123-4567;cic=+1-6789. At that provider the number is mapped to +1-202-533-1234, and the URI becomes tel:+1-202-533-1234.

For a ported geographical number +1-202-533-1234 with routing number 1-202-544-0000, the result is tel:+1-202-533-1234;npdi;rn=+1-202-544-0000. For a non-ported number +1-202-533-6789 the result is just tel:+1-202-533-6789;npdi.

The remaining examples cover errors. An invalid rn or cic may be dropped before querying the database again, and a freephone number that is one digit short has no CIC, so the call would be released.
sections.plainLanguage: A ported number gets an "already checked" tick and a note of where it lives now. A number that never moved just gets the tick. A toll-free number gets the name of the company that handles it.

sections.title: Security and the Circle of Trust
sections.content:
If rn or cic is changed illegally in transit, the call may be routed to the wrong network or node, causing call setup to be rejected. An illegally inserted npdi has the same effect. Illegally removing npdi is less of a problem, because an extra NP query can be done and the parameter added again. A tampered rn in the caller's URI would make charging based on it incorrect.

Because of this, the extensions apply only among nodes with mutual trust. A node that gets a request from an untrusted upstream node SHOULD remove the parameters, which generally causes it to redo its database queries. Call signaling protocols carrying them SHOULD provide hop-by-hop message integrity. For SIP, the RFC says this is accomplished with the SIPS URI mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could scribble on the sticky notes, calls could go to the wrong place. So you only believe the notes when they come from people you trust, and otherwise you peel them off and check again yourself.
